question: Who appoints notaries public in Florida?

options.why: Correct. Under §117.01 the Governor appoints Florida notaries; the Department of State's Notary Section processes commissions and keeps the records.
Wrong. Florida county clerks issue marriage licenses but don't appoint notaries.
Wrong. The Florida Bar regulates attorneys, not notaries.
Wrong. The Attorney General is the state's lawyer, not the appointing authority.

explanation: The Governor appoints Florida notaries; the Department of State handles commissioning and records.

question: How long is a Florida notary commission?

options.why: Correct. §117.01 sets a four-year term.
Wrong. Two years is half the Florida term.
Wrong. Six years is longer than the four-year term.
Wrong. Commissions expire after four years and must be renewed.

explanation: A Florida notary's term is four years.

question: What is the minimum age for a Florida notary?

options.why: Correct. §117.01 requires applicants to be at least 18.
Wrong. 21 isn't the Florida minimum; 18 is.
Wrong. 16-year-olds are minors and can't hold a commission.
Wrong. 25 is far above the statutory minimum of 18.

explanation: Applicants must be at least 18 years old.

question: Which is a Florida eligibility requirement?

options.text: Being a legal resident of Florida
options.why: Correct. §117.01 requires legal residence in Florida, plus age 18 and the ability to read, write and understand English.
Wrong. Florida doesn't require U.S. citizenship.
Wrong. No degree is required.
Wrong. Florida has no notary exam; it requires a course.

explanation: An applicant must be a legal resident of Florida, at least 18, and able to read, write and understand English.

question: What education must a first-time Florida applicant complete?

options.text: A three-hour interactive or classroom course within one year before applying
options.why: Correct. §117.01 requires first-time applicants to complete a three-hour interactive or classroom course within one year before applying.
Wrong. Six hours is California's requirement.
Wrong. Education is mandatory for first-time applicants.
Wrong. Forty hours is far beyond the three-hour requirement.

explanation: First-time applicants must complete a three-hour course within one year before applying.

question: What is the amount of the Florida notary bond?

options.why: Correct. §117.01 requires a $7,500 bond for a traditional commission.
Wrong. $10,000 is the Texas bond.
Wrong. $15,000 is the California bond.
Wrong. $25,000 is the bond for registered online notaries, not traditional ones.

explanation: A traditional Florida notary must post a $7,500 bond.

question: Does Florida require a state notary exam?

options.why: Correct. Florida requires the three-hour course but has no state exam.
Wrong. A 70% exam is California's or New York's requirement.
Wrong. Renewals don't involve an exam either.
Wrong. There's no exam online or in person.

explanation: Florida has no notary exam; first-time applicants take a three-hour course.

question: What language requirement applies to Florida applicants?

options.text: Must be able to read, write and understand English
options.why: Correct. §117.01 requires applicants to read, write and understand English.
Wrong. Bilingualism isn't required, though it can be useful.
Wrong. Spanish isn't required.
Wrong. There is an English-language requirement.

explanation: Applicants must be able to read, write and understand English.

question: An applicant has a felony conviction. What must be true for them to be appointed?

options.text: Their civil rights must have been restored, and the conviction must be disclosed
options.why: Correct. An applicant with a felony conviction must have had their civil rights restored and must disclose the conviction.
Wrong. Felonies matter; civil rights must be restored.
Wrong. Time alone doesn't satisfy the restoration requirement.
Wrong. Florida has no notary exam.

explanation: Applicants with felony convictions must have their civil rights restored and must disclose the conviction.

question: Where may a Florida notary perform notarial acts?

options.why: Correct. A Florida commission is valid throughout the state.
Wrong. Florida notaries aren't limited to their home county.
Wrong. Authority ends at the Florida state line.
Wrong. Florida notaries may act anywhere in the state, not only at work.

explanation: Florida notaries may act anywhere in Florida.

question: Who may suspend a Florida notary?

options.why: Correct. The Governor may suspend a notary on grounds in the Florida Constitution and chapter 117.
Wrong. County clerks have no suspension power.
Wrong. A surety can cancel the bond but can't suspend the commission.
Wrong. Suspension isn't done by any judge on their own initiative; it's the Governor's power.

explanation: The Governor may suspend a notary for misconduct and other grounds.
source: Fla. Stat. §117.01; Fla. Const. art. IV §7

question: A Florida notary changes their name. What must they do?

options.text: Request an amended commission from the Department of State and get a new seal
options.why: Correct. After a name change, the notary requests an amended commission from the Department of State and gets a new seal in the new name.
Wrong. The notary must sign in the commissioned name, so the commission must be amended.
Wrong. An amendment is enough; there's no need to reapply.
Wrong. The state, not the employer, keeps the commission record.

explanation: Name changes require an amended commission (and new seal) through the Department of State.

question: Must a Florida notary take an oath of office?

options.text: Yes, as part of the application
options.why: Correct. Applicants take an oath of office as part of the commissioning process.
Wrong. The oath is required.
Wrong. Every commission, new or renewed, requires the oath.
Wrong. All notaries are both bonded and sworn.

explanation: Applicants take an oath of office with their application.

question: A Florida notary moves out of state permanently. What happens?

options.text: They no longer meet the residency requirement and should resign the commission
options.why: Correct. Legal residency is a continuing requirement, so someone who moves out of state should resign the commission.

options.text: They may keep notarizing in Florida by visiting
options.why: Wrong. Visiting Florida doesn't restore residency.
Wrong. Commissions don't transfer between states.
Wrong. The notary no longer meets the residency requirement.

explanation: Moving out of Florida ends eligibility; the notary should resign.

question: Whom does the notary bond protect?

options.text: The public, against losses from the notary's misconduct
options.why: Correct. The bond protects members of the public harmed by the notary's breach of duty.
Wrong. A bond isn't insurance for the notary; the surety can seek repayment.
Wrong. The employer isn't the bond's beneficiary.
Wrong. The state isn't the beneficiary.

explanation: The bond protects members of the public harmed by the notary's breach of duty.

question: Is errors and omissions (E&O) insurance required for a traditional Florida notary?

options.text: No; it's optional for traditional notaries, though required for online notaries
options.why: Correct. Traditional notaries may buy E&O insurance voluntarily, but online notaries must carry at least $25,000.
Wrong. $7,500 is the traditional bond, which isn't E&O insurance.
Wrong. No $100,000 requirement exists.
Wrong. Only registered online notaries must carry E&O.

explanation: E&O insurance is optional for traditional notaries but required for online notaries.
